Main.sentence: Muammar Muhammad Abu Minyar al-Gaddafi [b] ( c. 1942 – 20 October 2011) was a Libyan military officer, ___E:revolutionary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutionary)___ , politician and political theorist who ruled ___E:Libya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libya)___ from 1969 until ___E:his assassination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_of_Muammar_Gaddafi)___ by Libyan ___E:rebel forces U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Gaddafi_forces)___ in 2011. He came to power through a ___E:military coup U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Libyan_revolution)___ , first becoming ___E:Revolutionary Chairman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutionary_Chairman_of_the_Libyan_Arab_Republic)___ of the ___E:Libyan Arab Republic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libyan_Arab_Republic)___ from 1969 to 1977, ___E:Secretary General of the General People's Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_General_of_the_General_People%27s_Congress)___ from 1977 to 1979, and then the ___E:Brotherly Leader U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brotherly_Leader_and_Guide_of_the_Revolution)___ of the ___E:Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Socialist_People%27s_Libyan_Arab_Jamahiriya)___ from 1979 to 2011. Initially ideologically committed to ___E:Arab nationalism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_nationalism)___ and ___E:Arab socialism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_socialism)___ , Gaddafi later ruled according to his own ___E:Third International Theory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_International_Theory)___ .

Born near ___E:Sirte U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirte)___ , ___E:Italian Libya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Libya)___ , to a poor ___E:Bedouin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedouin)___ ___E:Arab U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabs)___ family, Gaddafi became an Arab nationalist while at school in ___E:Sabha U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabha,_Libya)___ , later enrolling in the ___E:Royal Military Academy, Benghazi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benghazi_Military_University_Academy)___ .

He founded a revolutionary group known as the ___E:Free Officers movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Officers_movement_(Libya))___ which deposed the ___E:Western U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_world)___ -backed ___E:Senussi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senusiyya)___ monarchy of ___E:Idris U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idris_of_Libya)___ in a ___E:1969 coup U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Libyan_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat)___ .

Gaddafi converted Libya into a republic governed by his ___E:Revolutionary Command Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libyan_Revolutionary_Command_Council)___ . ___E:Ruling by decree U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_by_decree)___ , he ___E:deported Libya's Italian population U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_expulsion_of_Italians_from_Libya)___ and ejected its Western military bases.
He strengthened ties to Arab nationalist governments and unsuccessfully advocated ___E:pan-Arab political union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan-Arabism)___ .

An ___E:Islamic modernist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_modernism)___ , he introduced sharia as the basis for the legal system and promoted ___E:Islamic socialism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_socialism)___ .

He nationalized the oil industry and used the increasing state revenues to bolster the military, ___E:fund foreign revolutionaries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_relations_of_Libya_under_Muammar_Gaddafi#Support_for_rebel_and_paramilitary_groups)___ , and implement social programs emphasizing housebuilding, healthcare and education projects.

In 1973, he initiated a " ___E:Popular Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution_in_Libya)___ " with the formation of ___E:Basic People's Congresses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_People%27s_Congress_(political))___ , presented as a system of ___E:direct democracy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_democracy)___ , but retained personal control over major decisions.
He outlined his Third International Theory that year in The Green Book .
In 1977, Gaddafi transformed Libya into a new ___E:socialist state U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_state)___ called a Jamahiriya ("state of the masses").
He officially adopted a symbolic role in governance but remained head of both the military and the Revolutionary Committees responsible for policing and suppressing dissent.

During the 1970s and 1980s, Libya's unsuccessful border conflicts with ___E:Egypt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian%E2%80%93Libyan_War)___ and ___E:Chad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chadian%E2%80%93Libyan_conflict)___ , support for foreign militants, and alleged responsibility for bombings of ___E:Pan Am Flight 103 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_Am_Flight_103)___ and ___E:UTA Flight 772 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTA_Flight_772)___ left it increasingly isolated on the world stage.

A particularly hostile relationship developed with Israel, the United States and the United Kingdom, resulting in the ___E:1986 U.S. bombing of Libya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_United_States_bombing_of_Libya)___ and United Nations–imposed economic sanctions.

From 1999, Gaddafi shunned pan-Arabism, and encouraged ___E:pan-Africanism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan-Africanism)___ and rapprochement with ___E:Western nations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_nations)___ ; he was ___E:Chairperson of the African Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairperson_of_the_African_Union)___ from 2009 to 2010. Amid the 2011 ___E:Arab Spring U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Spring)___ , protests against widespread corruption and unemployment broke out in eastern Libya.

The situation descended into ___E:civil war U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libyan_Civil_War_(2011))___ , in which ___E:NATO U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO)___ ___E:intervened militarily U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_military_intervention_in_Libya)___ on the side of the anti-Gaddafist ___E:National Transitional Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Transitional_Council)___ (NTC).
Gaddafi's government was overthrown; he retreated to Sirte only to be captured, tortured and killed by NTC militants.
A highly divisive figure, Gaddafi dominated Libya's politics for four decades and was the subject of a pervasive ___E:cult of personality U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_of_personality)___ .

He was decorated with various awards and praised for his ___E:anti-imperialist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-imperialist)___ stance, support for Arab—and then African—unity, as well as for significant development to the country after the discovery of oil reserves.
Conversely, many Libyans strongly opposed Gaddafi's social and economic reforms; he was accused of various human rights violations.

He was condemned by many as a dictator whose ___E:authoritarian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarianism)___ administration systematically ___E:violated human rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_violations_during_the_Gaddafi_regime)___ and financed ___E:terrorism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorism)___ in the region and abroad.

Muammar Mohammed Abu Minyar al-Gaddafi  was born near ___E:Qasr Abu Hadi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qasr_Abu_Hadi)___ , a rural area outside the town of ___E:Sirte U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirte)___ in the deserts of ___E:Tripolitania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripolitania)___ , Italian western Libya.

His family came from a small, relatively uninfluential tribe called the ___E:Qadhadhfa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qadhadhfa)___ ,  who were ___E:Arab U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabs)___ in heritage.
His mother was Aisha bint Niran, and his father, Mohammad Abdul Salam bin Hamed bin Mohammad, was known as Abu Meniar; the latter earned a meager subsistence as a goat and camel herder.
Like other contemporary nomadic ___E:Bedouin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedouin)___ tribes, the family were illiterate and did not keep any birth records.

His birthday is not known with certainty and sources have set it in 1942 or the spring of 1943,  although his biographers ___E:David Blundy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Blundy)___ and ___E:Andrew Lycett U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Lycett)___ noted that it could have been pre-1940.  His parents' only surviving son, he had three older sisters.
Gaddafi's upbringing in Bedouin culture influenced his personal tastes; he preferred the desert over the city and would retreat there to meditate.

From childhood, Gaddafi was aware of the involvement of European colonial powers in Libya; his nation was ___E:occupied by Italy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Libya)___ , and during the ___E:North African Campaign U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_African_Campaign)___ of the ___E:Second World War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War)___ it witnessed conflict between Italian and British forces.

According to later claims, Gaddafi's paternal grandfather, Abdessalam Bouminyar, was killed by the Italian Army during the ___E:Italian invasion of 1911 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italo-Turkish_War)___ .
At the end of the Second World War in 1945, Libya was occupied by British and French forces.

Britain and France considered dividing the nation between their empires, but the ___E:General Assembly U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly)___ of the United Nations (UN) decided that the country was to be granted political independence,  and in 1951 created the ___E:United Kingdom of Libya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Libya)___ , a federal state under the leadership of a pro-Western monarch, ___E:Idris U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idris_of_Libya)___ , who banned political parties and centralized power in his own hands.
Gaddafi's earliest education was of a religious nature, imparted by a local Islamic teacher.
Subsequently, moving to nearby Sirte to attend elementary school, he progressed through six grades in four years.
Education in Libya was not free, but his father thought it would greatly benefit his son despite the financial strain.
During the week Gaddafi slept in a mosque, and only at weekends and holidays walked 20 miles (32 km) to visit his parents.
Even though Gaddafi's father was not educated, he made great sacrifices to send his son to school.
As an impoverished Bedouin, he faced bullying and discrimination from his city-dwelling classmates.
However, he had many Egyptian teachers who informed him of the dramatic events occurring in their homeland.

From Sirte, he and his family moved to the market town of ___E:Sabha U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabha,_Libya)___ in ___E:Fezzan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fezzan)___ , south-central Libya, where his father worked as a caretaker for a tribal leader while Muammar attended secondary school, something neither parent had done.  Gaddafi was popular at this school; some friends made there received significant jobs in his later administration, most notably his best friend, ___E:Abdul Salam Jalloud U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdessalam_Jalloud)___ .

Many teachers at Sabha were Egyptian, and for the first time, Gaddafi had access to pan-Arab newspapers and radio broadcasts, especially the ___E:Cairo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo)___ -based Voice of the Arabs .

Growing up, Gaddafi witnessed significant events severely disturb the ___E:Arab world U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_world)___ , including the ___E:1948 Arab–Israeli War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_Arab%E2%80%93Israeli_War)___ , the ___E:Egyptian Revolution of 1952 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_Revolution_of_1952)___ , the ___E:Suez Crisis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suez_Crisis)___ of 1956, and the short-lived existence of the ___E:United Arab Republic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Republic)___ (UAR) between 1958 and 1961.  Gaddafi admired the political changes implemented in the ___E:Arab Republic of Egypt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Republic_of_Egypt)___ under his hero, President ___E:Gamal Abdel Nasser U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamal_Abdel_Nasser)___ .

Nasser argued for ___E:Arab nationalism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_nationalism)___ ; the rejection of Western ___E:colonialism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonialism)___ , ___E:neo-colonialism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-colonialism)___ , and ___E:Zionism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zionism)___ ; and a transition from ___E:capitalism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism)___ to ___E:socialism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialism)___ .

Gaddafi was influenced by Nasser's book, Philosophy of the Revolution , which outlined how to initiate a coup.  One of Gaddafi's Egyptian teachers, Mahmoud Efay, was reportedly sympathetic towards the youth's political ideas, and advised him that a successful revolution would need the support of the army.
Gaddafi organized demonstrations and distributed posters criticizing the monarchy.
In October 1961, he led a demonstration protesting against Syria's secession from the UAR and raised funds to send cables of support to Nasser.
Twenty students were arrested as a result of the disorder.
Gaddafi and his companions also broke windows in a local hotel that was ___E:accused of serving alcohol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_dietary_laws#Intoxicants)___ .
To punish Gaddafi, the authorities expelled him and his family from Sabha.
Gaddafi moved to ___E:Misrata U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misrata)___ , there attending Misrata Secondary School.

Maintaining his interest in Arab nationalist activism, he refused to join any of the banned political parties active in the city—including the ___E:Arab Nationalist Movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Nationalist_Movement)___ , the ___E:Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libyan_Arab_Socialist_Ba%27ath_Party)___ , and the ___E:Muslim Brotherhood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Brotherhood)___ —claiming that he rejected factionalism.

He read voraciously on the subjects of Nasser and the ___E:French Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution)___ of 1789, as well as the works of the Syrian political theorist ___E:Michel Aflaq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Aflaq)___ and biographies of ___E:Abraham Lincoln U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln)___ , ___E:Sun Yat-sen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Yat-sen)___ , and ___E:Mustafa Kemal Atatürk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mustafa_Kemal_Atat%C3%BCrk)___ .

Gaddafi briefly studied history at the ___E:University of Libya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Libya)___ in ___E:Benghazi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benghazi)___ before dropping out to join the military.

Despite his police record, in 1963 he began training at the ___E:Royal Military Academy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benghazi_Military_University_Academy)___ , Benghazi, alongside several like-minded friends from Misrata.
The armed forces offered the only opportunity for upward social mobility for underprivileged Libyans, and Gaddafi recognized it as a potential instrument of political change.

Under Idris, Libya's armed forces were trained by the ___E:British Armed Forces U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Armed_Forces)___ ; this angered Gaddafi, who viewed the British as imperialists, and accordingly, he refused to learn English and was rude to the British officers, ultimately failing his exams.

British trainers reported him for insubordination and abusive behaviour, stating their suspicion that he was involved in the assassination of the military academy's commander in 1963. Such reports were ignored, and Gaddafi quickly progressed through the course. [contradictory]

With a group of loyal cadres, in 1964, Gaddafi established the Central Committee of the Free Officers Movement, a revolutionary group named after Nasser's ___E:Egyptian predecessor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Officers_Movement_(Egypt))___ .

Led by Gaddafi, they met secretively and were organized into a ___E:clandestine cell system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clandestine_cell_system)___ , pooling their salaries into a single fund.  Gaddafi travelled around Libya collecting intelligence and developing connections with sympathizers, but the government's intelligence services ignored him, considering him little threat.
Graduating in August 1965,  Gaddafi became a communications officer in the army's signal corps.

In April 1966, he was assigned to the United Kingdom for further training; over nine months he underwent an English-language course at ___E:Wilton Park U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilton_Park_Estate)___ in ___E:Beaconsfield U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaconsfield)___ , Buckinghamshire, an ___E:Army Air Corps U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_Air_Corps_(United_Kingdom))___ signal instructors course in ___E:Bovington Camp U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bovington_Camp)___ , Dorset, and an infantry signal instructors course at ___E:Hythe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hythe,_Kent)___ , Kent.  Despite later rumours to the contrary, he did not attend the ___E:Royal Military Academy Sandhurst U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Military_Academy_Sandhurst)___ .
The Bovington signal course's director reported that Gaddafi successfully overcame problems learning English, displaying a firm command of voice procedure.

Noting that Gaddafi's favourite hobbies were reading and playing ___E:football U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football)___ , he thought of him as an "amusing officer, always cheerful, hard-working, and conscientious".

Gaddafi disliked England, claiming ___E:British Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army)___ officers had racially insulted him and finding it difficult adjusting to the country's culture; asserting his Arab identity in London, he walked around ___E:Piccadilly U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piccadilly)___ wearing traditional Libyan robes.
He later related that while he travelled to England believing it more advanced than Libya, he returned home "more confident and proud of our values, ideals and social character".
People of Libya!

In response to your own will, fulfilling your most heartfelt wishes, answering your most incessant demands for change and regeneration, and your longing to strive towards these ends: listening to your incitement to rebel, your armed forces have undertaken the overthrow of the corrupt regime, the stench of which has sickened and horrified us all. At a single blow our gallant army has toppled these idols and has destroyed their images.

By a single stroke it has lightened the long dark night in which the Turkish domination was followed first by Italian rule, then by this reactionary and decadent regime which was no more than a hotbed of extortion, faction, treachery and treason.

Idris' government was increasingly unpopular by the latter 1960s; it had exacerbated Libya's traditional regional and tribal divisions by ___E:centralizing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_state)___ the country's ___E:federal system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federalism)___ to take advantage of the country's oil wealth.
Corruption and entrenched systems of patronage were widespread throughout the oil industry.

Arab nationalism was increasingly popular, and protests flared up after Egypt's 1967 defeat in the ___E:Six-Day War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six-Day_War)___ with Israel; Idris' administration was seen as pro-Israeli due to its alliance with the Western powers.
Anti-Western riots broke out in ___E:Tripoli U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripoli,_Libya)___ and Benghazi, while Libyan workers shut down oil terminals in solidarity with Egypt.

By 1969, the US ___E:Central Intelligence Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency)___ (CIA) was expecting segments of Libya's armed forces to launch a coup. Although claims have been made that they knew of Gaddafi's ___E:Free Officers Movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Officers_Movement_(Libya))___ , they have since claimed ignorance, stating that they were instead monitoring ___E:Abdul Aziz Shalhi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Abdul_Aziz_Shalhi&action=edit&redlink=1)___ 's Black Boots revolutionary group.

Shalhi, who effectively served as Idris' chief of staff, and his brother Omar were the sons of Idris' former chief advisor Ibrahim Shalhi, who had been murdered by ___E:Queen Fatima U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatimah_el-Sharif)___ 's nephew in the fall of 1954.  After their father's assassination, they became the favorites of Idris.
In mid-1969, Idris travelled abroad to spend the summer in Turkey and Greece amid widespread rumors of an abdication or a British-backed coup by the Shalhi brothers on 5 September.
Gaddafi's Free Officers, recognizing this as their last chance to preempt the Shelhis in overthrowing the monarchy, initiated "Operation Jerusalem".

If Gaddafi's Free Officers had not preempted the Shelhis, they would have almost certainly been defeated by the combined forces of Abdul Aziz Shelhi, the deputy commander of Libya's army, and the prominent families in ___E:Cyrenaica U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrenaica)___ that supported the Shelhi family.
On 1 September, Gaddafi's Free Officers occupied airports, police depots, radio stations, and government offices in Tripoli and Benghazi.

Gaddafi took control of the Berka barracks in Benghazi, while ___E:Umar Muhayshi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umar_Muhayshi)___ occupied Tripoli barracks and Jalloud seized the city's anti-aircraft batteries. ___E:Khweldi Hameidi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khweldi_Hameidi)___ took over the Tripoli radio station and was sent to arrest crown prince ___E:Sayyid Hasan ar-Rida al-Mahdi as-Sanussi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasan_as-Senussi)___ and force him to relinquish his claim to the throne.
They met no serious resistance and wielded little violence against the monarchists.
Once Gaddafi removed the monarchical government, he announced the foundation of the ___E:Libyan Arab Republic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Libya_under_Muammar_Gaddafi)___ .
Addressing the populace by radio, he proclaimed an end to the "reactionary and corrupt" regime, "the stench of which has sickened and horrified us all".
Due to the coup's bloodless nature, it was initially labelled the "White Revolution", although was later renamed the "One September Revolution" after the date on which it occurred.
Gaddafi insisted that the Free Officers' coup represented a revolution, marking the start of widespread change in the socio-economic and political nature of Libya.
He proclaimed that the revolution meant "freedom, socialism, and unity", and over the coming years implemented measures to achieve this.

The 12-member central committee of the Free Officers proclaimed themselves the ___E:Revolutionary Command Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libyan_Revolutionary_Command_Council)___ (RCC), the government of the new republic.

Lieutenant Gaddafi became RCC chairman, and therefore the de facto head of state, also appointing himself to the rank of ___E:colonel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonel)___ and becoming commander-in-chief of the armed forces.
Jalloud became Prime Minister,  while a civilian Council of Ministers headed by Sulaiman Maghribi was founded to implement RCC policy.
Libya's administrative capital was moved from ___E:al-Beida U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayda,_Libya)___ to Tripoli.
Although theoretically a collegial body operating through consensus building, Gaddafi dominated the RCC.  Some of the others attempted to constrain what they saw as his excesses.

Gaddafi remained the government's public face, with the identities of the other RCC members only being publicly revealed on 10 January 1970.  All young men from (typically rural) working and middle-class backgrounds, none had university degrees; in this way they were distinct from the wealthy, highly educated conservatives who previously governed the country.
The coup completed, the RCC proceeded with their intentions of consolidating the revolutionary government and modernizing the country.

They purged monarchists and members of Idris' ___E:Senussi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senussi)___ clan from Libya's political world and armed forces; Gaddafi believed this elite were opposed to the will of the Libyan people and had to be expunged.  ___E:People's Courts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libyan_People%27s_Court)___ were founded to try various monarchist politicians and journalists, many of whom were imprisoned, although none executed.
Idris was sentenced to execution in absentia .

Three months after Gaddafi came to power, the army minister and interior minister, both of whom were from the eastern ___E:Barqa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barqa)___ region, tried to overthrow him in a failed ___E:coup U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Libyan_coup_attempt)___ .

In 1970, Idris' great nephew ___E:Ahmed al-Senussi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmed_al-Senussi)___ tried to instigate another coup against Gaddafi; the ___E:monarchist plot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Prince_conspiracy)___ was foiled in August and Ahmed was sentenced to death (commuted in 1988 and pardoned by Gaddafi in 2001).

In May 1970, the Revolutionary Intellectuals Seminar was held to bring intellectuals in line with the revolution,  while that year's Legislative Review and Amendment united secular and religious law codes, introducing sharia into the legal system.  ___E:Ruling by decree U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_by_decree)___ , the RCC maintained the monarchy's ban on political parties, in May 1970 banned trade unions, and in 1972 outlawed workers' strikes and suspended newspapers.
In September 1971, Gaddafi resigned, claiming to be dissatisfied with the pace of reform, but returned to his position within a month.

In July 1972, amid widespread speculation that Gaddafi had been ousted or jailed by his political opponents, a new 18-man cabinet was formed with only two of them, Jalloud and ___E:Abdel Moneim al-Houni U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdel_Moneim_al-Houni)___ , being military men; the rest were civilian ___E:technocrats U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technocracy)___ per Gaddafi's insistence.
In February 1973, Gaddafi resigned again, once more returning the next month.
The RCC's early economic policy has been characterized as being ___E:state capitalist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_capitalism)___ in orientation.
Many initiatives were established to aid entrepreneurs and develop a Libyan bourgeoisie.

Seeking to expand the cultivatable acreage in Libya, in September 1969 the government launched a "Green Revolution" to increase agricultural productivity so that Libya could rely less on imported food.  The hope was to make Libya self-sufficient in food production.
All land that had either been expropriated from Italian settlers or which was not in use was repossessed and redistributed.
Irrigation systems were established along the northern coastline and around various inland oases.
Production costs often surpassed the value of the produce and thus Libyan agricultural production remained in deficit, relying heavily on state subsidies.
With ___E:crude oil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crude_oil)___ as the country's primary export, Gaddafi sought to improve Libya's oil sector.
In October 1969, he proclaimed the current trade terms unfair, benefiting foreign corporations more than the Libyan state, and threatened to decrease production.

In December Jalloud successfully increased the price of Libyan oil. On 2 March 1977, the General People's Congress adopted the " ___E:Declaration on the Establishment of the Authority of the People U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_on_the_Establishment_of_the_Authority_of_the_People)___ " at Gaddafi's behest.

Dissolving the Libyan Arab Republic, it was replaced by the Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya ( ___E:Arabic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language)___ : الجماهيرية العربية الليبية الشعبية الاشتراكية , al-Jamāhīrīyah al-‘Arabīyah al-Lībīyah ash-Sha‘bīyah al-Ishtirākīyah) , a "state of the masses" conceptualized by Gaddafi.

A new, all-green banner was adopted as the country's flag.  Officially, the Jamahiriya was a ___E:direct democracy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_democracy)___ in which the people ruled themselves through the 187 ___E:Basic People's Congresses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_People%27s_Congress_(political))___ (BPCs), where all adult Libyans participated and voted on national decisions.
These then sent members to the annual General People's Congress, which was broadcast live on television.
In principle, the People's Congresses were Libya's highest authority, with major decisions proposed by government officials or with Gaddafi himself requiring the consent of the People's Congresses.
Gaddafi became General Secretary of the GPC, although he stepped down from this position in early 1979 and appointed himself "Leader of the Revolution".
Although all political control was officially vested in the People's Congresses, in reality Libya's existing political leadership continued to exercise varying degrees of power and influence.
Debate remained limited, and major decisions regarding the economy and defence were avoided or dealt with cursorily; the GPC largely remained "a rubber stamp" for Gaddafi's policies.

On rare occasions, the GPC opposed Gaddafi's suggestions, sometimes successfully; notably, when Gaddafi called on primary schools to be abolished, believing that ___E:homeschooling U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_schooling)___ was healthier for children, the GPC rejected the idea.  In other instances, Gaddafi pushed through laws without the GPC's support, such as when he desired to allow women into the armed forces.
At other times, he ordered snap elections when it appeared that the GPC would enact laws he opposed.

Gaddafi proclaimed that the People's Congresses provided for Libya's every political need, rendering other political organizations unnecessary; all non-authorized groups, including political parties, professional associations, independent trade unions, and women's groups, were banned.
Despite these restrictions, St. John noted that the Jamahiriya system still "introduced a level of representation and participation hitherto unknown in Libya".

With preceding legal institutions abolished, Gaddafi envisioned the Jamahiriya as following the ___E:Qur'an U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qur%27an)___ for legal guidance, adopting sharia law; he proclaimed "man-made" laws unnatural and dictatorial, only permitting ___E:Allah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_in_Islam)___ 's law.  Within a year he was backtracking, announcing that sharia was inappropriate for the Jamahiriya because it guaranteed the protection of private property, contravening The Green Book 's socialism.
His emphasis on placing his own work on a par with the Qur'an led conservative clerics to accuse him of shirk , furthering their opposition to his regime.
In July 1977, a ___E:border war broke out U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian%E2%80%93Libyan_War)___ with Egypt, in which the Egyptians defeated Libya despite their technological inferiority.
The conflict lasted one week before both sides agreed to sign a peace treaty that was brokered by several Arab states.
Both Egypt and Sudan had aligned themselves with the US, and this pushed Libya into a strategic, although not political, alignment with the Soviet Union.

In recognition of the growing commercial relationship between Libya and the Soviets, Gaddafi was invited to visit Moscow in December 1976; there, he entered talks with ___E:Leonid Brezhnev U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonid_Brezhnev)___ .

In August 1977, he visited ___E:Yugoslavia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia)___ , where he met its leader ___E:Josip Broz Tito U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josip_Broz_Tito)___ , with whom he had a much warmer relationship.

He also enjoyed a warm relationship with ___E:Romanian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Republic_of_Romania)___ leader ___E:Nicolae Ceaușescu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolae_Ceau%C8%99escu)___ .
According to Romanian spy chief ___E:Ion Mihai Pacepa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion_Mihai_Pacepa)___ , Gaddafi once exclaimed to Ceaușescu, "My brother!

You are my brother for the rest of my life!"  After Pacepa defected to the US in July 1978, Gaddafi and ___E:Yasser Arafat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasser_Arafat)___ contributed $1 million each to Ceaușescu's $4 million bounty on Pacepa.
If socialism is defined as a redistribution of wealth and resources, a socialist revolution clearly occurred in Libya after 1969 and most especially in the second half of the 1970s.
The management of the economy was increasingly socialist in intent and effect with wealth in housing, capital and land significantly redistributed or in the process of redistribution.
Private enterprise was virtually eliminated, largely replaced by a centrally controlled economy.

In December 1978, Gaddafi stepped down as Secretary-General of the GPC, announcing his new focus on revolutionary rather than government activities; this was part of his new emphasis on separating the apparatus of the revolution from government.
Although no longer in a formal government post, he adopted the title of "Leader of the Revolution" and continued as commander-in-chief of the armed forces.

Historian Dirk Vandewalle stated that despite the Jamahariya's claims to being a direct democracy, Libya remained "an exclusionary political system whose decision-making process" was "restricted to a small cadre of advisers and confidantes" surrounding Gaddafi.
Libya turned towards socialism.

In March 1978, the government issued guidelines for housing redistribution, attempting to ensure every adult owned their own home. Most families were banned from owning more than one house, while former rental properties were expropriated by the state and sold to the tenants at a heavily subsidized price.

In September, Gaddafi called for the People's Committees to eliminate the "bureaucracy of the public sector" and the "dictatorship of the private sector"; the People's Committees took control of several hundred companies, converting them into ___E:worker cooperatives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worker_cooperative)___ run by elected representatives.

In March 1979, the GPC announced the separation of government and revolution, the latter being represented by new Revolutionary Committees, who operated with the People's Committees in schools, universities, unions, the police force, and the military.
Dominated by revolutionary zealots, mostly youths, the Revolutionary Committees were based in Tripoli and met with Gaddafi annually.
Membership was drawn from within the BPCs.  The revolutionary committee system became "a key—if not the main—mechanism through which [Gaddafi] exercises political control in Libya".
Publishing a weekly magazine, The Green March , starting October 1980 they took control of the press.

Responsible for perpetuating the revolution, they performed ideological surveillance, adopting a significant security role, making arrests and putting people on trial according to the "law of the revolution".

With no legal or safeguards, the administration of revolutionary justice was largely arbitrary and resulted in widespread abuse and the suppression of ___E:civil liberties U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_liberties)___ : the "Green Terror".

In 1979, the committees began the redistribution of land in the ___E:Jefara U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jafara)___ plain, continuing through 1981.  In May 1980, measures to redistribute and equalize wealth were implemented; anyone with over 1000 ___E:dinar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libyan_dinar)___ in their bank account saw that extra money expropriated.

The next year, the GPC announced that the government would take control of all import, export and distribution functions, with state supermarkets replacing privately owned businesses; this led to a decline in the availability of consumer goods and the development of a thriving ___E:black market U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_market)___ .
Gaddafi was frustrated by the slow pace of social reform on women's issues, and in 1979 launched a Revolutionary Women's Formation, to replace the more gradualist Libyan General Women's Federation.
In 1978 he had established a Women's Military Academy in Tripoli, encouraging all women to enlist for training.

The measure was hugely controversial and voted down by the GPC in February 1983. Gaddafi remained adamant, and when it was again voted down by the GPC in March 1984, he refused to abide by the decision, declaring that "he who opposes the training and emancipation of women is an agent of imperialism, whether he likes it or not."
The Jamahiriya's radical direction earned the government many enemies.

Most internal opposition came from ___E:Islamic fundamentalists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_fundamentalism)___ , inspired by the events of the 1979 ___E:Iranian Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Revolution)___ .
In February 1978, Gaddafi discovered that his head of military intelligence was plotting to kill him and increasingly entrusted security to his Qadhadfa tribe.
Many who had seen their wealth confiscated turned against the administration, and Western-funded opposition groups were founded by exiles.

Most prominent was the ___E:National Front for the Salvation of Libya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Front_for_the_Salvation_of_Libya)___ (NFSL), which orchestrated militant attacks against Libya's government.
Another, al-Borkan, began killing Libyan diplomats abroad.
Following Gaddafi's command to kill these "stray dogs", the Revolutionary Committees set up overseas branches to suppress counter-revolutionary activity, assassinating dissidents.

Although Syria and Israel also employed hit squads, Gaddafi was unusual in publicly bragging about his use of them;  in April 1980, he ordered all dissidents to return home by 10 June or be "liquidated wherever you are".

Within a three months period in 1980, at least ten Libyan dissidents were murdered in Europe, including ex-diplomats, ex-army officers, businessmen, journalists, and student activists in disparate locations such as ___E:London U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London)___ , ___E:Greece U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece)___ and ___E:Austria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria)___ .

In 1984, Gaddafi was tricked by Egyptian President ___E:Hosni Mubarak U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hosni_Mubarak)___ into announcing the assassination of former Libyan Prime Minister ___E:Abdul Hamid al-Bakkoush U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdul_Hamid_al-Bakkoush)___ in Cairo; Bakkhoush not only turned up alive but held a press conference with Egypt's Interior Minister.

The early 80s saw economic trouble in Libya; from 1982 to 1986, annual oil revenues dropped from $21 to $5.4 billion.

Focusing on irrigation projects, 1983 saw construction start on Libya's largest and most expensive infrastructure project, the ___E:Great Man-Made River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Man-Made_River)___ ; although designed to be finished by the end of the decade, it remained incomplete at the start of the 21st century.

Domestic threats continued to plague Gaddafi; in May 1984, his ___E:Bab al-Azizia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bab_al-Azizia)___ home was unsuccessfully attacked by a militia—linked to the NFSL or Muslim Brotherhood—and in the aftermath 5,000 dissidents were arrested.

Ishkal's death was attributed to ___E:Jalloud U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdessalam_Jalloud)___ , Khalifa Hunaysh or Gaddafi.

Libya had long supported the ___E:FROLINAT U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FROLINAT)___ militia in neighbouring Chad, but FROLINAT became divided over its ties to Libya in 1976. In January 1978, the anti-Libya faction within FROLINAT, led by ___E:Hissène Habré U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiss%C3%A8ne_Habr%C3%A9)___ , switched sides and allied with Chadian President ___E:Félix Malloum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%A9lix_Malloum)___ .

Meanwhile, the pro-Libya faction within FROLINAT, led by ___E:Goukouni Oueddei U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goukouni_Oueddei)___ , renamed itself ___E:People's Armed Forces U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Armed_Forces)___ (FAP).

In December 1980, Gaddafi reinvaded Chad at the request of the FAP-controlled ___E:GUNT government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transitional_Government_of_National_Unity_(Chad))___ to aid in the civil war; in January 1981, Gaddafi suggested a political merger.

The ___E:Organisation of African Unity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_African_Unity)___ (OAU) rejected this and called for a Libyan withdrawal, which came in November 1981. The civil war resumed, and Libya sent troops back in.
In 1982, the GUNT government was overthrown by Habré's forces and Oueddei fled to Libya, where Gaddafi provided him with arms to continue to guerrilla war against Habré.

In November 1984, Gaddafi met with French President ___E:François Mitterrand U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Mitterrand)___ ; both agreed to withdraw from Chad.  Oueddei broke with Gaddafi in 1985 due to the former's intentions to negotiate a truce with Habré.
Consequently, he was placed under house arrest by Gaddafi and allegedly arrested by Libyan police and shot in the stomach.
Oueddei survived the shooting and fled to Algeria, but continued to claim he and Gaddafi enjoyed a good relationship.

When Gaddafi ordered the remnant of GUNT to attack Habré in February 1986 in violation of his agreement with Mitterrand, France launched ___E:Operation Épervier U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_%C3%89pervier)___ , which escalated into the ___E:Toyota War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota_War)___ .

Libya suffered a humiliating defeat as it was completely expelled from Chad and its commander ___E:Khalifa Haftar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalifa_Haftar)___ captured, along with 600-700 Libyan soldiers.

Gaddafi disavowed Haftar and the other prisoners; one possible contributing factor to this repudiation may have been that Gaddafi had signed an agreement to withdraw Libyan forces, and Haftar's operations had been in violation of this.   An embittered Haftar then joined the anti-Gaddafi ___E:National Front for the Salvation of Libya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Front_for_the_Salvation_of_Libya)___ , became a CIA asset, and was given refuge in the US.

Many African nations were tired of Libya's interference in their affairs; by 1980, nine African states had severed diplomatic relations,  while in 1982 the OAU cancelled its scheduled conference in Tripoli to prevent Gaddafi gaining chairmanship.

Some African states, such as ___E:Jerry Rawlings U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Rawlings)___ 's Ghana and ___E:Thomas Sankara U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Sankara)___ 's Burkina Faso, had warm relations with Libya during the 1980s.

Proposing political unity with Morocco, in August 1984, Gaddafi and Moroccan monarch ___E:Hassan II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_II_of_Morocco)___ signed the ___E:Oujda Treaty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oujda_Treaty)___ , forming the Arab–African Union; such a union was considered surprising due to the political differences and longstanding enmity that existed between the two. In a sign of warming relations, Gaddafi promised to stop funding the ___E:Polisario Front U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polisario_Front)___ and Hassan II extradited former RCC member ___E:Umar Muhayshi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umar_Muhayshi)___ to Libya, where he was immediately killed.
But relations deteriorated, particularly due to Morocco's friendship with the US and Israel; in August 1986, Hassan abolished the union.
Angered by the snub, Gaddafi plotted with ___E:Abu Nidal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Nidal)___ to assassinate Hassan in 1987, but the plot was aborted.

In 1981, the new US president, ___E:Ronald Reagan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan)___ , pursued a hardline approach to Libya, viewing it as a ___E:puppet regime U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puppet_regime)___ of the Soviet Union.
Gaddafi played up his commercial relationship with the Soviets, revisiting Moscow in 1981 and 1985,  and threatening to join the ___E:Warsaw Pact U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact)___ .
The Soviets were nevertheless cautious of Gaddafi, seeing him as an unpredictable extremist.
In August 1981, the US staged military exercises in the Gulf of Sirte – an area which Libya claimed.

The US ___E:shot down U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Sidra_incident_(1981))___ two Libyan ___E:Su-22 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhoi_Su-17)___ planes which were on an intercept course.
Closing down Libya's embassy in Washington, Reagan advised US companies operating in Libya to reduce Americans stationed there.

In December 1981, the ___E:White House U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House)___ claimed Gaddafi had dispatched a hit squad to assassinate Reagan, allegedly led by ___E:Carlos the Jackal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_the_Jackal)___ , who had been living in Libya under Gaddafi's protection after the 1975 ___E:OPEC siege U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OPEC_siege)___ .

Secretary of State ___E:Alexander Haig U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Haig)___ , Defense Secretary ___E:Caspar Weinberger U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspar_Weinberger)___ , Counselor to the President ___E:Edwin Meese U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Meese)___ , chief of staff ___E:James Baker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Baker)___ , and deputy chief of staff ___E:Michael Deaver U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Deaver)___ were considered potential targets and given special security.

US ambassador to Italy ___E:Maxwell M. Rabb U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell_M._Rabb)___ , who was Jewish, was urgently recalled due to threats against his life. Gaddafi denied the allegations.

Gaddafi was accused of having ties to the ___E:Lebanese Armed Revolutionary Factions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanese_Armed_Revolutionary_Factions)___ , which had murdered US ___E:military attaché U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_attach%C3%A9)___ ___E:Charles R. Ray U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_R._Ray)___ and Israeli diplomat ___E:Yacov Barsimantov U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_of_Yacov_Barsimantov)___ in Paris.

In spring 1986, ___E:the US Navy again performed exercises in the Gulf of Sirte U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_in_the_Gulf_of_Sidra_(1986))___ ; the Libyan military retaliated, but failed as the US sank Libyan ships.

Diplomatic relations also broke down with the UK, after Libyan diplomats were accused in the killing of ___E:Yvonne Fletcher U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yvonne_Fletcher)___ , a British policewoman stationed outside their London embassy, in April 1984.

In 1980, Gaddafi hired former CIA agent ___E:Edwin P. Wilson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_P._Wilson)___ , living in Libya as a fugitive from US justice, to plot the murder of an anti-Gaddafi Libyan graduate student at ___E:Colorado State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_University)___ named Faisal Zagallai.

In 1984, Gaddafi publicly ___E:executed Al-Sadek Hamed Al-Shuwehdy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Execution_of_Al-Sadek_Hamed_Al-Shuwehdy)___ , an aeronautical engineer studying in the US.

Reagan was supported by the UK, but opposed by other European allies, who argued it contravened international law.  In ___E:Operation El Dorado Canyon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_United_States_bombing_of_Libya)___ , orchestrated on 15 April 1986, US military planes launched air-strikes, bombing military installations, killing around 100 Libyans, including civilians.
